content: Apnea of prematurity is a frequent issue observed in preterm infants within neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). This condition often delays the discharge of these infants to their homes or their transfer to less intensive care settings. Preterm infants are particularly susceptible to carnitine deficiency, which has led to the use of carnitine supplementation as a potential preventive and therapeutic intervention for apnea. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether carnitine supplementation could reduce the frequency of apneic episodes, shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation, and decrease the length of hospital stay in preterm infants experiencing recurrent apnea. To address this, independent computerized searches were conducted by two reviewers. The databases searched included MEDLINE (from 1966 to December 2010), EMBASE (from 1988 to December 2010), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, Issue 2, 2010). Additionally, abstracts from annual meetings of the Society for Pediatric Research (spanning 1995 to 2010) were reviewed, and subject matter experts were contacted for further insights. The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving preterm infants diagnosed with recurrent apnea of prematurity. Eligible trials needed to compare carnitine treatment with either a placebo or no treatment and assess at least one of the following outcomes: failure to resolve apneas, duration of mechanical ventilation, or length of hospital stay. Two reviewers independently assessed the identified studies for inclusion and quality. When necessary, corresponding authors of the studies were contacted to obtain additional information. No trials meeting the eligibility criteria were identified during the review process. The authors concluded that, although there is a plausible theoretical basis for using carnitine to treat apnea of prematurity, the current evidence is insufficient to support its use for this purpose. Further research is required to clarify the potential role of carnitine supplementation in the clinical management of this condition.
